**Key Concepts:**
- People with equal capacity should pay the same
- People with greater ability should pay more
- Focuses on distributive nature of taxation

presentation_slides.title: Horizontal and Vertical Equity
presentation_slides.content:
**The ability-to-pay approach is based on two principles:**

**1. Horizontal Equity:**
- People in the same circumstances should pay the same taxes
- Equal treatment of equals

**Example:**
- Two people with the same income should pay the same tax

**2. Vertical Equity:**
- Degree of proportionality is important
- Unequals should be treated unequally
- People with different incomes should pay different taxes

**Example:**
- Higher-income person pays more tax than lower-income person

presentation_slides.title: Types of Taxes by Impact
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Progressive Tax:**
- Higher incomes pay a higher share of taxes
- Average tax rate rises with income
- People with higher incomes pay a higher percentage

**Example:** Income tax brackets (10% for low income, 35% for high income)

**2. Proportional Tax:**
- Everyone pays the same share of taxes
- Average tax rate is the same at all income levels

**Example:** Flat tax rate of 15% on all incomes

**3. Regressive Tax:**
- Those with high income pay a lower share of income
- Average tax rate falls when income rises

**Example:** Sales tax (8% on a $100 purchase = 8% of income for a person earning $1,000; 0.8% for a person earning $10,000)

presentation_slides.title: Measuring Ability to Pay
presentation_slides.content:
**Question:** How is the ability to pay measured?

**Ideal Measure:**
- Reflects entire welfare a person can derive
- Includes consumption (present and future)
- Holding of wealth
- Enjoyment of leisure

**Limitation:**
- Such a comprehensive measure is not practicable

**Practical Approach:**
- Use income as a proxy
- Income is observable and measurable
- Income correlates with ability to pay

**Challenge:**
- Income may not fully reflect ability to pay
- Wealth and consumption also matter
- But income is the most practical measure

sections.section_title: Tax System and Structure in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Section 5.3: Tax System and Structure in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Explain the tax system in Ethiopia
- Explain various tax policies

presentation_slides.title: History and Legal Framework
presentation_slides.content:
**History:**
- 1944: Emperor issued decree requiring peasants to pay one-tenth of agricultural products

**Current Legal Framework:**
- Proclamation No. 33/1992
- FDRE Constitution (1995)

**Responsible Agency:**
- Federal Ministry of Revenues (MoR)

**Revenue Sharing (Constitution):**
- Federal government levies taxes on federal revenue sources
- Regional states levy taxes on state revenue sources
- Federal government administers federal budget
- Regional states administer state budgets

**Current Federal Structure:**
- 11 regional states
- 2 autonomous administrations (Addis Ababa, Dire Dawa)

sections.section_title: Types of Tax and Tax Accounting in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Section 5.4: Types of Tax and Tax Accounting
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Describe the various types of taxes in Ethiopia
- Explain various tax policies of Ethiopia
- Understand the different tax schedules and rates

presentation_slides.title: Schedules of Income in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**According to Tax Proclamation No. 286/2002:**

**Schedule A: Income from Employment**
- Tax rates: 10% to 35%
- Withheld by employers (final tax)
- Includes: salary, wages, allowances, bonus, commission, gratuity
- Includes value of fringe benefits
- Termination payments

**Schedule B: Income from Rental of Buildings**
- Tax on income from renting buildings
- Gross income reduced by allowable deductions

**Schedule C: Income from Business**
- Tax on income earned from businesses
- Total business income reduced by deductions

**Schedule D: Other Income**
- Royalties
- Income from services rendered outside Ethiopia
- Income from games, dividends
- Casual rental income, interest income
- Specified non-business capital gains

**Schedule E: Exempt Income**
- Medical treatment costs, hardship allowance
- Domestic servant salaries, maintenance/child support
- Travel expenses for recruited employees
- Pension contributions, compensation payments

sections.section_title: Types of Tax and Tax Accounting in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Employment Income Tax Rates (Table 5.1)
presentation_slides.content:
**Monthly Employment Income Tax Rates in Ethiopia:**

| Monthly Employment Income (Birr) | Tax Rate |
|----------------------------------|----------|
| 0 - 600 | 0% |
| 601 - 1,650 | 10% |
| 1,651 - 3,200 | 15% |
| 3,201 - 5,250 | 20% |
| 5,251 - 7,800 | 25% |
| 7,801 - 10,900 | 30% |
| More than 10,900 | 35% |

**Source:** Ethiopian Investment Commission (2020)

presentation_slides.title: Indirect Taxes in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Value Added Tax (VAT):**
- Introduced: 1 January 2003
- Standard rate: 15%
- Applied on every taxable transaction by registered persons
- Destination-based/consumption tax
- VAT must be included in selling price
- Exemptions exist (supplier doesn't levy VAT)

**2. Turnover Tax (TOT):**
- Equalization tax on persons not registered for VAT
- For annual transactions > 500,000 Birr (VAT registration threshold)
- Rate: 2% on goods, 10% on services
- Applied to contractors, grain mills, tractors, combine harvesters (2%)

**3. Excise Tax:**
- On selected goods (luxury, inelastic demand, hazardous to health)
- 19 groups of items, 378 goods
- Rate: 5% to 500%
- Payable on import (at customs) or local production (within 30 days)

presentation_slides.title: More Indirect Taxes in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**4. Surtax:**
- Additional 10% tax on imported goods
- Exemptions: fertilizers, petroleum, lubricants, motor vehicles, aircraft, spacecraft, capital goods
- Ministry of Finance can adjust exempt list

**5. Withholding Tax:**
- All bodies and specified sole proprietors must deduct
- Rate: 2% of value of domestic transactions
- Remit to tax authority monthly

**6. Stamp Duty:**
- Tax raised by requiring stamps on designated documents
- Official mark/seal indicating tax payment
- Form of revenue for government treasury

**7. Customs Duty:**
- Tax on imported or exported goods
- Instrument to prevent/reduce importation
- Serves as trade barrier
- Can reach 100% or above
- Protects infant domestic industries

presentation_slides.title: Summary of Taxes (Table 5.3)
presentation_slides.content:
**Summary of Taxes in Ethiopia:**

| Tax Type | Rate | Frequency |
|----------|------|-----------|
| Business Income Tax | 30% (bodies), 10-35% (individuals) | Annual/Monthly |
| Employment Income Tax | 10-35% progressive | Monthly |
| Rental Income Tax | 25% of taxable income | Annual |
| Value Added Tax (VAT) | 15% | Monthly/Quarterly |
| Turnover Tax (TOT) | 2% (goods), 10% (services) | Annual/Quarterly |
| Excise Tax | 5-500% | Monthly/on import |
| Surtax | 10% | On import |
| Withholding Tax | 2% | Monthly |

**Sources:** Ethiopian Investment Commission (2020)

presentation_slides.title: Tax and Accounting
presentation_slides.content:
**Tax Accounting in Ethiopia:**

- All taxation involves accounting processes
- Tax accounting is used by individuals, businesses, and other entities

**For Individuals:**
- Focuses on income, qualifying deductions, investment gains/losses
- Employees in public establishments have income tax paid by employers

**For Businesses:**
- Need to keep up-to-date financial records
- Helps determine tax liabilities

**Key Point:**
- Tax and accounting are two separate but linked entities
- Financial statements are used to make tax calculations

sections.section_title: Problems Associated with Taxation in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Section 5.5: Problems Associated with Taxation
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Explain prevailing problems of taxation in Ethiopia
- Suggest possible remedial actions to alleviate the problems

**Key Questions:**
- What are the major criticisms of tax systems?
- What are the problems specific to Ethiopian taxation?

presentation_slides.title: Common Problems in Tax Systems
presentation_slides.content:
**Major Criticisms of Tax Systems Worldwide:**

1. **Complexity of administration**
2. **Difficulty for taxpayers to understand and comply**

**Consequences:**
- Taxpayers incur costs to correctly calculate tax liability
- Encourages growth of unreported transactions (underground economy)
- Encourages demand for tax shelters

**In Developed Countries:**
- Focus on modernizing customer services
- "Client orientation" approach
- New management techniques

presentation_slides.title: Problems in Developing Countries
presentation_slides.content:
**In Developing Countries (including Ethiopia):**

1. **Complexity of the tax system**
2. **Perception of corruption**
3. **Cost of compliance**
4. **Fairness perception of the tax system**
5. **Lack of tax knowledge**
   - Has a positive effect on voluntary tax compliance

**Key Categories:**
- Tax compliance problems
- Bureaucracy in tax systems

**Tax Compliance:**
- Degree to which taxpayers comply with tax laws
- Tax non-compliance: Tax avoidance and tax evasion

presentation_slides.title: Tax Avoidance vs. Tax Evasion
presentation_slides.content:
**Tax Avoidance:**

**Definition:** Arranging one's affairs to minimize the tax burden.

**Methods:**
- Taking full advantage of tax code provisions
- Using exemptions, deductions, or incentives

**Status:**
- **Not illegal**
- But poses problems for tax administration

**Tax Evasion:**

**Definition:** Falsifying information on a tax return to reduce tax liability or not filing at all.

**Methods:**
- Underreporting income
- Overstating deductions
- Not declaring income
- Not filing returns

**Status:**
- **Illegal**
- Punishable by law

**Rooted in underground economic activities:**
- Illegal activities (no records wanted)
- High marginal tax rates (incentive to avoid reporting)

presentation_slides.title: Other Tax Administration Problems
presentation_slides.content:
**Additional Problems in Ethiopia and Elsewhere:**

1. **Steadily growing workload**
2. **Complexity of fiscal legislation**
3. **Attitude of taxpayers**
4. **Degree of non-compliance**
5. **Need to improve customer service**
6. **Need to reduce costs of tax assessment and collection**
7. **Need for efficient and effective management**

**Key Questions:**
- How can efficiency and effectiveness of tax collection be improved?
- How can tax awareness be increased?

**Suggested Solutions:**
- Simplification of tax system
- Increasing transparency
- Improving taxpayer education
- Modernizing tax administration

sections.section_title: Concept of Poverty and Its Measurement

presentation_slides.title: Unit 6: Poverty and Inequality
presentation_slides.content:
Welcome to Unit 6! In this unit, we will explore:
- The concept of poverty and its measurement
- The concept of inequality and its measurement
- Global and regional poverty
- Women and poverty
- Poverty and inequality in Ethiopia
- The role of indigenous knowledge in reducing poverty

presentation_slides.title: Section 6.1: Concept of Poverty
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Explain the meaning of poverty
- Describe how poverty can be measured

**Quotes from the Poor:**
- "When one is poor, she has no say in public, she feels inferior. She has no food, so there is famine in her house." - Poor woman from Uganda
- "...low salaries and lack of jobs. And it's not having medicine, food, and clothes." - Discussion group in Brazil
- "Life is so precarious that the youth... must migrate to the towns or join the army... to escape the hazards of hunger." - Discussion group in rural Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Dimensions of Poverty (Poor People's Definition)
presentation_slides.content:
**Six Dimensions of Poverty:**

1. **Multiple Interlocked Dimensions:**
   - Lack of food (bottom line: hunger)
   - Lack of many things simultaneously

2. **Psychological Dimensions:**
   - Powerlessness, voicelessness
   - Dependency, shame, humiliation
   - Cultural identity and social norms help maintain humanity

3. **Lack of Access to Basic Infrastructure:**
   - Roads (especially in rural areas)
   - Transportation
   - Clean water

4. **Education:**
   - Widespread thirst for literacy
   - Education offers escape from poverty
   - Quality must improve

5. **Poor Health:**
   - Dreaded everywhere as a source of destitution
   - Costs of health care
   - Income lost due to illness

6. **Managing Assets:**
   - Physical, human, social, environmental
   - Way to cope with vulnerability
   - Has a gender dimension

presentation_slides.title: Definitions of Poverty
presentation_slides.content:
**World Bank Definition (2000):**
Poverty is "the pronounced deprivation in wellbeing."

**Wellbeing Seen from Three Angles:**

1. **Conventional View (Monetary):**
   - Wellbeing linked to command over commodities
   - Poor = Not enough income/consumption above a minimum threshold

2. **Specific Consumption:**
   - People could be house poor, food poor, or health poor

3. **Capability View:**
   - Focuses on the capability of the individual to function in society
   - Poor people often lack key capabilities
   - Inadequate income, education, poor health
   - Feel powerless, lack political freedoms

presentation_slides.title: 6.1.2 Types of Poverty
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Relative Poverty:**
- Defined in comparison to others' standing in the economy
- Can meet basic needs but still poor relative to others
- Observed within a society or internationally
- Most relevant in societies without acute absolute poverty
- Matter of distributive justice

**2. Absolute Poverty:**
- Unable or only barely able to meet subsistence essentials
- Deprivation of basic needs: food, clothing, shelter
- Expressed as number of people below a minimum level of real income
- International poverty line: $1.25 per day or $2 per day
- Failure of basic dignity or human rights

**Other Dimensions:**
- Disproportionately located in rural areas
- Primarily engaged in agriculture
- More likely to be women and children than adult males
- Often concentrated among minority ethnic groups and indigenous peoples

presentation_slides.title: 6.1.3 Measuring Poverty
presentation_slides.content:
**Four Reasons to Measure Poverty:**

1. **Keep poor people on the agenda**
2. **Identify poor people** (to target appropriate interventions)
3. **Monitor and evaluate projects and policy interventions**
4. **Evaluate the effectiveness of institutions**

**Three Steps to Measure Poverty:**

1. **Define an indicator of welfare** (income or consumption)
2. **Establish a poverty line** (minimum acceptable standard)
3. **Generate a summary statistic** (aggregate information)

**Common Implementation:**
- Fixed, monetary, consumption-based threshold
- Data from household survey
- Poverty measured as percentage with per capita consumption below poverty line

presentation_slides.title: Common Poverty Measures
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Poverty Headcount Index (H):**
- H = Number of people below poverty line / Total population
- Also called "headcount ratio"
- Simple to understand but doesn't show depth of poverty

**2. Total Poverty Gap (TPG):**
- Total amount of income needed to raise everyone below poverty line to that line
- Sum of differences between poverty line and actual incomes of the poor

**3. Average Poverty Gap (APG):**
- TPG / Total population

**4. Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) Index:**
- Measures degree of income inequality among the poor
- Helps understand depth and severity of poverty

**These are unidimensional measures (based on income).**

presentation_slides.title: Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
The MPI is the most prominent application of multidimensional poverty measurement, incorporating three dimensions at the household level.

**Three Dimensions and Their Indicators:**

**1. Health (2 indicators):**
- Whether any child has died in the family
- Whether any adult/child in the family is malnourished
- Each counts 1/6 toward MPI

**2. Education (2 indicators):**
- Whether even one household member has completed 5 years of schooling
- Whether any school-age child (grades 1-8) is out of school
- Each counts 1/6 toward MPI

**3. Standard of Living (6 indicators):**
- Lack of electricity
- Insufficiently safe drinking water
- Inadequate sanitation
- Inadequate flooring
- Lack of cooking fuel
- Lack of assets

Each indicator is weighted equally (1/6 for health and education, 1/18 for each living standard indicator)

presentation_slides.title: 6.1.4 Sen's Approach to Poverty and Wellbeing
presentation_slides.content:
**Key Proponent:** Amartya Sen (1998 Nobel Laureate in Economics)

**Critique of Traditional Welfare Economics:**
- Traditional approach stresses revealed preferences (desire-based utilities)
- Lacks enough information about people's preferences to assess social good

**Alternative: Capability Approach**
- Relies not on individuals' attainments (e.g., of basic needs)
- Relies on individuals' capabilities

**Key Concepts:**
- Income and wealth are not ends in themselves
- They are instruments for other purposes
- Capability to function is what really matters for one's status as poor or non-poor
- Expansion of commodity production is valued as a means to human welfare and freedom

presentation_slides.title: Sen's Capability Approach - Key Ideas
presentation_slides.content:
**What Matters:**
- Not what a person has
- But what a person is, or can be
- And does, or can do

**Not Just Characteristics of Commodities:**
- Example: A book is of little value to an illiterate person (except as cooking fuel)
- Need to think beyond availability of commodities
- Address their use (functionings)

**Functionings:**
- What a person does or can do with commodities of given characteristics

**Capabilities:**
- Real freedoms that people have to achieve their potential doings and beings

**Conversion Factors:**
- Personal, socio-political, and environmental conditions
- Determine whether someone can convert resources into functionings

**Human Wellbeing:**
- Being healthy, well-nourished, well-clothed
- Literate, long-lived
- Able to take part in community life
- Being mobile, having freedom of choice
- Lack of these = deficiency in wellbeing = poverty

sections.section_title: Concept of Inequality and its Measurements

presentation_slides.title: Section 6.2: Concept of Inequality
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Explain the meaning of inequality
- Analyse the measurements of inequality
- Understand functional and personal distribution of income
- Interpret Lorenz Curves and the Gini Coefficient

presentation_slides.title: Definition and Types of Inequality
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Inequality refers to the situation of being unequal or uneven, or a social disparity of distribution or opportunity.

**Dimensions of Inequality:**
- Economic
- Social
- Political

**Examples:**
- Inequality of power
- Inequality of prestige
- Inequality of status
- Gender inequality
- Job satisfaction, conditions of work
- Degree of participation
- Freedom of choice

**Focus Here:**
Economic (mainly income) dimension

presentation_slides.title: Types of Income Distribution
presentation_slides.content:
**Economic Inequality:**
The disproportionate distribution of total national income among households.

**Two Types of Income Distribution:**

**1. Functional/Factor Share Distribution:**
- Shares of total national income each factor of production receives
- Labour share (wages, salaries)
- Land share (rent)
- Capital share (interest, profit)
- Attempts to explain incomes by contribution to production

**2. Personal/Size Distribution:**
- Most commonly used indicator
- Deals with individual persons or households
- Total incomes received regardless of source
- Arranged from lowest to highest income

presentation_slides.title: Measuring Income Distribution
presentation_slides.content:
**Steps in Measuring Personal Income Distribution:**

1. Arrange all individuals by ascending personal incomes
2. Divide population into quintiles (fifths) or deciles (tenths)
3. Determine what proportion of total national income is received by each income group

**Table 6.1: Typical Size Distribution of Personal Income**

| Individuals | Personal Income | Share of Total Income (%) |
|-------------|-----------------|---------------------------|
| 1-4 (bottom 20%) | 5 units | 5% |
| 5-8 (second 20%) | 9 units | 9% |
| 9-12 (third 20%) | 14 units | 14% |
| 13-16 (fourth 20%) | 21 units | 21% |
| 17-20 (top 20%) | 51 units | 51% |
| **Total** | **100 units** | **100%** |

**Kuznets Ratio:**
- Ratio of incomes received by top 20% to bottom 40%
- Example: (51 / 14) = 3.64
- Higher ratio = More inequality

presentation_slides.title: Lorenz Curve
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
The Lorenz curve shows cumulative shares of income received by individuals or groups.

**How to Construct:**
- Horizontal axis: Number of income recipients in cumulative percentage (0-100%)
- Vertical axis: Share of income received by each group (0-100%)

**Figure 6.1: The Lorenz Curve**

**Interpretation:**
- 45-degree diagonal line = Perfect equality
  - 50% of population receives 50% of income
  - 75% of population receives 75% of income
- More bowed out curve = More inequality
- Actual Lorenz curves lie between 45-degree line and complete inequality

**Figure 6.2: The Lorenz Curve and Gini Coefficient**

presentation_slides.title: Gini Coefficient
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
The Gini coefficient is a numerical measure of income inequality derived from the Lorenz curve.

**Calculation:**
- G = Area A / (Area A + Area B)
- Where A = area between the Lorenz curve and the 45-degree line
- B = area below the Lorenz curve

**Range of Gini Coefficient:**

| Value | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| G = 0 | Perfect equality (everyone has same income) |
| 0 < G < 1 | Some inequality (most real-world cases) |
| G = 1 | Perfect inequality (one person has all income) |

**Examples:**
- Country A: G = 0.28 → Relatively equal distribution
- Country B: G = 0.60 → Highly unequal distribution
- Higher Gini coefficient = Higher inequality

presentation_slides.title: Interpreting the Gini Coefficient
presentation_slides.content:
**Gini Coefficient Values Around the World:**

**Most Equal Countries (Low Gini):**
- Nordic countries: ~0.25
- Several European countries: ~0.25-0.35

**Most Unequal Countries (High Gini):**
- South Africa: ~0.63
- Namibia: ~0.59
- Brazil: ~0.53

**Ethiopia (2014/15):**
- National: 0.33
- Rural: 0.38
- Urban: 0.28

**Key Points:**
- Gini coefficient is the most widely used measure of income inequality
- Can be used to compare inequality across countries
- Can track changes in inequality over time

**Limitation:**
- Doesn't show where along the income distribution the inequality exists

presentation_slides.title: Section 6.3: Global and Regional Poverty
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Recognise the situation of poverty from global and regional perspectives
- Explain why extreme poverty still remains a challenge in parts of the world
- Understand the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)

presentation_slides.title: Global Poverty Trends
presentation_slides.content:
**Progress Over the Past Half Century:**
- Extreme poverty declined from 36% (1990) to 10% (2015)
- Significant progress in countries like China
- Millions lifted out of poverty

**Persistent Challenges:**
- 1.2+ billion people lived on less than $1.25/day in 2010
- 2.4 billion lived on less than $2/day (more than 1/3 of world population)
- 700+ million people (10% of world population) living in extreme poverty
- Majority of those on less than $1.90/day live in Sub-Saharan Africa

**Regional Variation:**
- Sub-Saharan Africa: Virtually no rate reduction from 1950-2000
- Asia: Significant progress
- Latin America: Mixed results

presentation_slides.title: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
presentation_slides.content:
**SDGs 2015-2030:**

**Goal 1:** No Poverty

**Goal 2:** Zero Hunger

**Goal 3:** Good Health and Well-Being

**Goal 4:** Quality Education

**Goal 5:** Gender Equality

**Goal 6:** Clean Water and Sanitation

**Goal 7:** Affordable and Clean Energy

**Goal 8:** Decent Work and Economic Growth

**Goal 9:** Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure

**Goal 10:** Reduced Inequality

**Goal 11:** Sustainable Cities and Communities

**Goal 12:** Responsible Consumption and Production

**Goal 13:** Climate Action

**Goal 14:** Life below Water

**Goal 15:** Life on Land

**Goal 16:** Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions

**Goal 17:** Partnerships to Achieve the Goals

presentation_slides.title: Poverty Reduction Strategies
presentation_slides.content:
**Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP):**
- Framework promoted by the World Bank
- Helps countries think systematically about how to improve the position of poor people
- Many developing countries have undergone this process

**Key Focus Areas:**
- Economic growth
- Investment in human capital
- Social protection
- Good governance
- Infrastructure development

**Ethiopia:**
- Has undergone the PRSP process
- Conducts regular Household Income and Consumption Expenditure Surveys (HICES)
- Welfare Monitoring Surveys (WMS) established in 1996
- Prepares Poverty Analysis Reports

**Inequality is Rising Globally:**
- Due to globalization
- Technical progress
- Policies and institutions of different countries

presentation_slides.title: Section 6.4: Women and Poverty
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Appreciate why some groups in society such as women face poverty
- Identify measures to address the problem of poverty facing women

presentation_slides.title: Women and Poverty - Key Facts
presentation_slides.content:
**Globally:**
- Women make up a substantial majority of the world's poor
- Among poorest communities, women and children experience the harshest deprivation
- Women are more likely to be poor and malnourished
- Women less likely to receive medical services, clean water, sanitation

**Reasons:**
1. **Prevalence of female-headed households**
2. **Lower earning capacity of women**
3. **Limited control over spouses' income**
4. **Less access to education**
5. **Less access to formal-sector employment**
6. **Less access to social security**
7. **Less access to government employment programmes**

**Urban Areas:**
- Women less likely to obtain formal employment
- Frequently restricted to illegal, low-productivity jobs

**Rural Areas:**
- Women have less access to resources
- Social customs and laws restrict property ownership

presentation_slides.title: Intra-Household Inequalities
presentation_slides.content:
**Household Income Alone is Misleading:**
- Higher proportion of female-headed households in poorest areas
- Less access to public services (water, sanitation, health care)
- Household members more likely to fall ill
- Children in female-headed households less likely to be enrolled in school
- More likely to be working to provide additional income

**Intra-Household Resource Allocation:**
- Bias against females in:
  - Nutrition
  - Medical care
  - Education
  - Inheritance

**Economic Status of Women Matters:**
- Where women's share of income is relatively high
  - Less discrimination against girls
  - Women better able to meet their own needs and those of their children
- When income is marginal
  - Women contribute larger fraction of income to household nutrition
  - Rise in male earnings leads to less than proportionate increase in funds for daily needs

presentation_slides.title: Reasons for Limited Control Over Resources
presentation_slides.content:
**Why Women Have Limited Control Over Household Income and Resources:**

1. **Unremunerated Work:**
   - Large proportion of women's work is unpaid
   - Collecting firewood and cooking
   - Parenting (intangible)

2. **Unpaid Work in Family Agriculture or Business:**
   - Many women from poor households are not paid
   - Common for male head to control all funds

**Perpetuation of Inequality:**
- Public programmes working exclusively with men exacerbate inequalities
- Training programmes geared to men
- Agricultural extension programmes promote male-dominated crops

**Consequences:**
- Women's economic status remains low
- Control over household resources is limited

presentation_slides.title: Policy Implications
presentation_slides.content:
**Design of Development Policy:**
- Must integrate women into development programmes
- Particularly important for women and children welfare

**Specific Actions:**
1. **Increase female participation rates in:**
   - Educational and training programmes
   - Formal-sector employment
   - Agricultural extension programmes

2. **Ensure equal access to:**
   - Government resources
   - Schooling
   - Health and other services

3. **Formalize/legalize informal sector employment**
   - Majority of female labour force employed in informal sector
   - Will improve economic status of women

4. **Challenge basic assumptions**
   - Women-centered poverty strategies
   - Crucial role women play in community's escape from poverty

presentation_slides.title: Long-Term Implications
presentation_slides.content:
**Ethical Implications:**
- Any process of growth that fails to improve the welfare of the poorest has failed to accomplish one of the principal goals of development

**Economic Implications:**
- Low status of women translates into slower rates of economic growth

**Benefits of Investing in Women:**
- Benefits of current investments in human capital are more likely to be passed onto future generations
- Human capital is the most important prerequisite for growth
- Education and enhanced economic status for women are critical

**Key Conclusion:**
- Women must be drawn into the economic mainstream
- This is essential for improving living conditions for the poorest individuals

sections.section_title: Overview of Poverty and Inequalities in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Section 6.5: Overview of Poverty in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Recognise the extent of poverty and inequality in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Poverty in Ethiopia - Key Facts
presentation_slides.content:
**Population:**
- 118 million people (as of 2021)

**Economic Growth:**
- Average 9.8% per year (2008/09 to 2018/19)
- Strong, broad-based growth

**Poverty Reduction:**
- Population below national poverty line declined from 38% to 24%
- Headcount poverty declined from 59% (1992) to 29.5% (2011)

**Remaining Challenges:**
- Ethiopia remains one of the poorest countries in the world
- Per capita annual income: $883 (MoFEC, 2019)

**Human Development Index (HDI):**
- 0.485 (2019)
- Position: 173 out of 189 countries
- Low human development category

**Poverty Lines:**
- 44% earn less than $1/day
- 89% fall below $2/day poverty line

presentation_slides.title: Rural Poverty in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**Food Insecurity:**
- More than 12 million people are chronically or periodically food insecure (IFAD)

**Rural Livelihoods:**
- Most poor people live in rural areas
- Per capita income: Less than $0.50/day
- Majority are smallholder farmers

**Vulnerability:**
- Depend on rain-fed agriculture
- Exposed to climate-related vulnerabilities
- Inadequate health and education systems
- Poor access to basic services

**Poverty Trends:**
- Poverty has generally decreased
- Still a challenge, especially in rural areas
- Rate of decrease is slower in rural than urban areas

presentation_slides.title: Poverty Monitoring in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**Government Monitoring Systems:**

**Household Income and Consumption Expenditure Surveys (HICES):**
- Conducted regularly by Central Statistical Agency
- Provides data on income and consumption

**Welfare Monitoring Survey (WMS):**
- Established in 1996
- Monitors welfare indicators

**Poverty Analysis Report:**
- Prepared by Ministry of Finance and Economic Development (MoFED)
- Provides status and trends of:
  - National-level poverty incidence
  - Rural and urban poverty
  - Regional-level poverty
  - Poverty gap and severity
  - Income inequality (Gini coefficient)

**World Bank PRSP Process:**
- Ethiopia pursues this framework

sections.section_title: Role of Indigenous Knowledge in Reducing Poverty

presentation_slides.title: Section 6.6: Role of Indigenous Knowledge
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Appreciate the role of indigenous knowledge and practices in reducing poverty
- Identify different local actors and actions that work to improve the wellbeing of society

presentation_slides.title: What is Indigenous Knowledge?
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Indigenous knowledge is the accumulated set of common-sense knowledge and ideas of local people about their everyday realities of living, unique to a given community.

**Also Known As:**
- Traditional knowledge
- Local knowledge
- Traditional wisdom

**Characteristics:**
- Locally based
- Developed within communities
- Used to solve problems within society
- Dynamic (evolves over time)
- Practices serve as pooling resources for a common good

**Purpose:**
- Used to solve different problems
- Including relief of poverty

**Ethiopia:**
- Endowed with diverse cultures and peoples
- Rich in indigenous knowledge and associated practices
- Some unique to specific localities, others common to wider environment

presentation_slides.title: Idir - Traditional Burial Association
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
The most common informal institution in Ethiopia. A form of burial society that provides support and consolation in times of death and grief.

**Characteristics:**
- Association established among neighbours or workers
- Raises funds for emergencies (death within groups)
- Group life insurance
- Large membership
- Weekly/monthly membership minimal and affordable

**Functions:**
- Guarantees grieving families complete assistance
- Financial support for burial ceremony
- Members required to attend funerals
- Must be ready to help with burial ceremony

**Types:**
- Community/village-based
- Workplace-based
- Among friends and family

**Slogan:** "Idir for mutual benefits, to lessen societal burden."

presentation_slides.title: Iqub - Rotating Credit Association
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
A rotating credit association established by a small group of people to provide substantial funding for members to improve their lives.

**Also Called:** "Ikub"

**How It Works:**
- Savings club
- Each member contributes weekly or monthly
- Pool of money is collected
- Members take turns receiving the full amount

**Benefits for Poor Families:**
- Obtain funding for:
  - Weddings
  - Building a house
  - Starting a small business
- More flexible and accessible than banks
- Minimal paperwork
- People without formal education not discouraged

**Characteristics:**
- Small regular payments
- Steady flow of money
- Rotational basis
- Temporary or permanent (depending on needs)

presentation_slides.title: Other Informal Associations
presentation_slides.content:
**Debo (Work Group):**
- Community members assist an individual on a rotational basis
- Often free of charge
- Usually organised by men
- Pool labour to work on each other's farmland
- Rotational basis

**Characteristics of Iqub and Idir:**
- Informal, bottom-up
- Widely practiced socio-economic traditions
- Serve needs of society in a sustainable way
- Based on available human or material resources

**Benefits:**
- Everyone taken care of in times of need
- Participatory and enabling means
- Community kept intact
- Grieving family instantly gets financial and social support

**Values Promoted:**
- Accountability
- Transparency
- Tolerance
- Dialogue
- Friendship among members
- Strong ties discourage defaults

presentation_slides.title: Cottage Industry
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Small-scale, decentralized manufacturing units using conventional and low-technology methods.

**Location:**
Often operated out of a home rather than a purpose-built facility.

**Characteristics:**
- Defined by investment required to start
- Number of people employed

**Examples in Ethiopia:**
- Weaving
- Leather working
- Pottery
- Basket making
- Blacksmithing
- Agricultural, household, and construction equipment

**Advantages:**
- Labour-intensive techniques
- Provide employment
- Reduce unemployment
- Offer self-employment opportunities for men and women

**Contribution:**
- Significant contribution to local and national economies
- Backbone of many rural economies

**Other Actors:**
- Modern cooperatives (e.g., coffee unions)
- Key vehicles for poverty reduction
- Sustainable livelihood development

sections.section_title: National Development Objectives and Strategies - Historical Review

presentation_slides.title: Unit 7: Macroeconomic Reforms in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
Welcome to Unit 7! In this unit, we will explore:
- National development objectives and strategies (historical review)
- Development plans during the Imperial period
- Development plans under the Socialist period (Derg)
- Development plans under FDRE (EPRDF)
- Home-grown economic reforms
- Fiscal decentralization

presentation_slides.title: Section 7.1: Historical Review
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Identify national development plan objectives and strategies
- Analyse the national development plans of the Monarchy, Military, and EPRDF governments

**Historical Context:**
- Ethiopia is the oldest independent country in Africa
- Ancient monarchy maintained freedom from colonial rule (except 1936-1941)
- 1974: Derg deposed Emperor Haile Selassie I
- 1991: EPRDF toppled the Derg
- 1994: Constitution adopted
- 1995: First multiparty election held

presentation_slides.title: 7.1.1 Imperial Period (1950-74)
presentation_slides.content:
**First Five-Year Plan (1957-1961):**

**Main Objectives:**
- Development of strong infrastructure (transportation, construction, communication)
- Establishment of skilled and semi-skilled personnel for processing industries
- Acceleration of agricultural development through commercial ventures

**Results:**
- GNP increased at 3.2% (target: 3.7%)
- Agriculture, manufacturing, mining failed to meet targets
- Exports grew at 3.5%, imports at 6.4% per annum
- Failed to correct negative balance of trade (since 1951)
- Coffee accounted for 70% of foreign exchange earnings

presentation_slides.title: Second and Third Five-Year Plans
presentation_slides.content:
**Second Five-Year Plan (1962-1967):**

**Objectives:**
- Change from agricultural to agro-industrial economy
- Diversification of production
- Introduction of modern processing methods
- Expansion of productive capacity
- Large-scale commercial farms promoted over subsistence farms

**Third Five-Year Plan (1968-1973):**

**Objectives:**
- Raising manufacturing and agro-industrial performance
- Expansion of educational opportunities
- Improvement in peasant agriculture
- Shifted focus to agricultural sector (food shortages)

**Results:**
- 1960-1970: Annual average growth rate of 4% in per capita GDP
- Manufacturing growth rate doubled (1.9% to 4.4%)
- Services sector grew (9.3% to 15.6%)

**Failure:**
- Feudal land tenure system deprived millions of peasants
- Failed to improve lives of most Ethiopians
- Overthrow of monarchy in 1974

presentation_slides.title: 7.1.2 Socialist Period (Derg, 1974-1991)
presentation_slides.content:
**Key Policies:**
- Socialist state established
- Centrally planned economy
- Industry-led development
- Nationalization of rural land and productive assets
- Land distributed among farmers
- Commercial farms put under government control
- Land tenancy abolished
- Private commercial labourers marginalized
- Large collectivization programmes
- Overvalued currency
- Marketing and pricing policies
- Agricultural Marketing Corporation (AMC) established

**Four Phases:**

**I. 1974-1978:**
- Little economic growth
- Nationalization caused economic dislocation
- Military budget consumed substantial resources
- GDP growth: 0.4% average annual

presentation_slides.title: Derg Period - Phases II and III
presentation_slides.content:
**II. 1978-1980:**
- Economy began to recover
- Government consolidated power
- "Development through Cooperation Campaign" (Zemecha)
- GDP growth: 5.7% average annual
- Agriculture: 3.6% (good weather)
- Manufacturing: 18.9%

**III. 1980-1985:**
- Economy experienced setback
- GDP declined, manufacturing downturn
- Agriculture reached crisis stage

**Four Reasons:**
1. Widespread drought
2. Manufacturing sector stagnated (agricultural inputs declined)
3. Lack of foreign exchange and declining investment
4. Rise in defense expenditure

presentation_slides.title: Derg Period - Phase IV
presentation_slides.content:
**IV. 1985-1990:**

**Ten-Year Perspective Plan (1984-1994):**
- Development of agriculture
- Enhancement of exports
- Improvement in quality of livestock

**Strategies:**
- Cooperativisation
- Establishment of state farms

**Results:**
- Agricultural decline reversed
- Manufacturing sector grew
- GDP increased: 5% average annual

**Challenges:**
- Lingering effects of 1984/85 droughts
- Contributed to overall stagnation

**End of Derg:**
- Toppled by EPRDF in 1991

presentation_slides.title: 7.1.3 FDRE Period - ADLI Strategy
presentation_slides.content:
**EPRDF Rise to Power (1991):**
- Considerable shift in development strategies
- Moved from centrally planned industrial development to agricultural-led development

**Key Policy Changes:**
- Agricultural price controls removed
- State farm assets privatized
- Export-oriented development strategy
- Structural Adjustment Programmes (SAPs) implemented

**Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization (ADLI) - 1994:**

**Main Objective:**
- Attain food self-sufficiency by increasing agricultural productivity and output

**Three Main Strategies:**
1. Expansion of agricultural technologies
2. Investment in agricultural infrastructure and inputs
3. Boosting rural non-agricultural sectors

**Wider Programmes:**
- Investment in infrastructure (roads, telecommunication, electricity)
- Enhancing flow of finance
- Local governments' administrative capacity
- Agro-processing industries

presentation_slides.title: ADLI Implementation
presentation_slides.content:
**Key Programmes under ADLI:**
- Rural Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVETs)
- Development of water resources (hydro power and irrigation)
- Improvements in microfinance institutions
- Marketing of agricultural products
- Restructuring of smallholder cooperatives

**Participatory Demonstration and Training Extension System (PADETES):**
- Used to distribute fertilizers, seed, and credit
- Spread information on better agricultural practices

**ADLI Framework:**
- Remains key pillar for successive development plans:
  1. SDPRP (Sustainable Development and Poverty Reduction Programme)
  2. PASDEP (Plan for Accelerated and Sustained Development to End Poverty)
  3. GTP I (Growth and Transformation Plan I)
  4. GTP II (Growth and Transformation Plan II)

presentation_slides.title: Peace, Democracy and Development Programme
presentation_slides.content:
**Five-Year Development Program:**

**Major Goals and Objectives:**

1. **Poverty alleviation through rapid economic growth**

2. **Ensuring peace and security by:**
   - Strengthening political system that promotes people's equality and fraternity
   - Guaranteeing administrative justice
   - Peaceful coexistence with neighbouring countries

3. **Laying groundwork for:**
   - Attainment of MDGs by 2015
   - People-oriented development

**Vision:**
- Build an economy with:
  - Modern and productive agricultural sector
  - Industrial sector that plays a leading role
- Sustain economic development and secure social justice
- Increase per capita income to middle-income country level by 2025

presentation_slides.title: PASDEP (2005/06-2009/10)
presentation_slides.content:
**Eight Strategic Goals:**

1. Building all-inclusive implementation capacity
2. Massive push to accelerate economic growth
3. Balance between economic development and population growth
4. Unleashing the potentials of Ethiopia's women
5. Strengthening infrastructural backbone
6. Strengthening human resource development
7. Managing risk and volatility
8. Creating employment opportunities

**Two Growth Scenarios:**

| Scenario | Growth Target | Purpose |
|----------|---------------|---------|
| Base Case | 7% per annum | Achieve MDGs |
| High Case | 10% per annum | Beyond MDGs, foundation for vision |

**PASDEP:** Ethiopia's second poverty reduction strategy, built on SDPRP directions.

presentation_slides.title: GTP I (2010/11-2014/15)
presentation_slides.content:
**Third National Development Plan:**

**Four Overarching Objectives:**

1. Maintaining at least 11% average real GDP growth per annum and attaining MDGs by 2014/15

2. Expanding access and ensuring quality of education and health services (achieving MDGs in social sectors)

3. Establishing conditions for sustainable nation building through stable democratic and developmental state

4. Ensuring sustainability of growth through maintaining macroeconomic stability

**Seven Pillar Strategies:**
- Cut across all socio-economic sectors

**Agricultural Focus:**
- Identify and scale up smallholders' best practices
- Introduce new agricultural technologies
- Support small-scale farmers through training and fertilizer provisions
- Promote high-value crops

**Industrialization:**
- Labour-intensive manufacturing
- Import substitution and export-oriented industrialization

presentation_slides.title: GTP II (2015/16-2019/20)
presentation_slides.content:
**Overarching Objective:**
Sustain accelerated growth and establish a springboard for economic structural transformation.

**Specific Objectives:**

1. Achieve 11% average real GDP growth within stable macroeconomic environment

2. Develop domestic engineering and fabrication capacity

3. Improve productivity, quality, and competitiveness of productive sectors

4. Solidify public mobilization and participation

5. Deepen hegemony of developmental political economy

**Eight Pillar Strategies:**
1. Sustain rapid, broad-based, equitable economic growth
2. Increase productive capacity and efficiency
3. Speed up transformation of private sector
4. Build capacity of domestic construction industry
5. Manage rapid urbanization
6. Accelerate human development and technological capacity
7. Establish democratic and developmental good governance
8. Promote women and youth empowerment
9. Build a climate resilient green economy

sections.section_title: Overview of Home-grown Economic Reforms in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Section 7.2: Home-grown Economic Reforms
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Explain the home-grown economy reforms and the needs for reform
- Understand the rationale and objectives of HGER
- Identify the components of HGER (macroeconomic, sectoral, structural reforms)

presentation_slides.title: Rationale for Home-grown Economic Reforms
presentation_slides.content:
**Why Reform Was Needed:**

**Growth Pattern 2010-2020:**
- Rapid growth driven by aggregate demand
- Large-scale government-funded infrastructure developments
- Financed through heavy debt and external aid

**Problems:**
1. Continuous inflationary pressures
2. Failure to raise productivity
3. Failure to create adequate job opportunities
4. Heavy debt burden making growth unsustainable

**Need for New Approach:**
- New growth financing approach
- Moving away from heavy reliance on public spending and debt financing

**Home-Grown Economic Reform (HGER):**
- Domestically initiated
- Central objectives:
  1. Sustaining rapid growth
  2. Maintaining stable macroeconomic environment (reducing debt vulnerabilities)
  3. Creating adequate and sustainable job opportunities

presentation_slides.title: Classification of HGER
presentation_slides.content:
**The HGER Plan Has Three Components:**

**1. Macroeconomic Reforms:**
- Focus on eliminating macroeconomic imbalances
- Strict macroeconomic management
- Key focus areas:
  - Ensuring fast, sustainable, and broad-based economic growth
  - Fiscal policy reform (modernizing tax collection, public expenditure management)
  - Financial sector reform (ensuring financial stability, inclusion)
  - Foreign exchange reform (expanding inflow of foreign currencies)
  - External public debt management (minimizing commercial loans, rescheduling)

**2. Sectoral Reforms:**
- Multi-sectoral growth approach
- Diversifying sources of growth and job creation
- Focus sectors:
  - Agriculture
  - Manufacturing
  - Mining
  - Tourism
  - ICT

presentation_slides.title: HGER - Structural Reforms
presentation_slides.content:
**3. Structural Reforms:**

**Key Objectives:**
- Government intervention should not crowd out private investors
- Encourage private sector participation
- Support all development forces based on merits and performance

**Focus Areas:**

1. **Ensuring coordinated transport and logistics services:**
   - Reducing transit time and trade costs
   - Improving competitiveness of products
   - Improving quality and effectiveness of transport corridors

2. **Implementing import substituting development strategy:**
   - Substitute import of strategic commodities
   - Focus: food items, edible oil, wheat
   - Domestic production

3. **Reforming investment and job creation landscape:**
   - Industrial parks to maximum capacity utilization
   - Improving investment and business environment
   - Eliminating unnecessary bureaucracy
   - Improving finance supply (Ease of Doing Business initiative)

presentation_slides.title: Structural Reforms (Continued)
presentation_slides.content:
4. **Increasing role and participation of private sector:**
   - Examine challenges faced by private sector
   - Create favourable conditions
   - Make bureaucracy support and encourage investors
   - Make Ethiopia a start-up nation for investment and job creation

5. **Expediting privatization of large state-owned enterprises:**
   - Liberalization of selected sectors
   - Expected to improve efficiency and quality of growth

6. **Strengthening Ethiopia's global and regional partnership:**
   - WTO accession negotiations
   - African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) ratification
   - Develop cross-country infrastructure with neighbours
   - Reduce transportation and trade costs
   - Ensure shared prosperity

7. **Promoting free movement of labour:**
   - Design mechanisms for free mobility of skilled labour
   - Domestically and internationally

presentation_slides.title: Structural Reforms (Further)
presentation_slides.content:
8. **Promoting development of civic societies:**
   - Conducive environment for civic societies
   - Role in economic, social, and political activities
   - Facilitates genuine transition to democracy
   - Includes media
   - Builds political economic outlook
   - Citizens' political and moral authority

9. **Diversifying Ethiopia's development partnerships and sources of development finances:**
   - Domestic policy reforms
   - Strong relationship and partnership with development actors
   - Secure different sources of development finance

**Key Point:**
- Development does not focus only on incomplete material being
- Expands to multifaceted freedoms for complete meaning

presentation_slides.title: Section 7.3: Fiscal Decentralization
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Understand the concept of fiscal decentralization
- Discuss fiscal equalization
- Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of decentralized systems

presentation_slides.title: Concept of Fiscal Decentralization
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Fiscal decentralization is the transfer of fiscal responsibilities (spending and revenue) from the central government to lower levels of government.

**Centralization Ratio:**
- Direct government expenditure by central government / Total government expenditure
- Excludes federal grants/transfers
- Measures extent of centralization

**Fiscal Equalization in Ethiopia:**
- Federal government makes fiscal equalization payments to local governments
- Stated goal: Equalizing fiscal capacity of local governments to provide services
- Helps regional governments provide similar sets of public services
- Similar tax incidence

**Fiscal Equalization Aims:**
- Reduce or eliminate differences in net fiscal benefits
- Net fiscal benefits = Utility from public services - Taxes paid

**Companion of Fiscal Decentralization:**
- Ensures equity, efficiency, and stability of fiscal policy

presentation_slides.title: Fiscal Decentralization in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**Past Ten Years (2010-2020):**
- Additional budgetary support for regional governments
- Finance capital projects
- Help achieve MDGs and SDGs

**Example (2017/18):**
- Birr 7 billion allocated to regional states
- Grant formula for SDG implementation
- Enhanced fiscal equalization
- Narrow regional disparities in basic social services:
  - Education
  - Health
  - Water and sanitation

presentation_slides.title: 7.3.1 Disadvantages of Decentralized System
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Interstate/Local Externalities:**
- Costs and benefits of local goods/services to residents in other jurisdictions
- Creates problems for efficient operation of federal system
- Example: Education, sewage

**2. Loss of Scale Economies in Provision of Public Goods:**
- Cost per person may fall as number of users increases
- Example: Public library
- Each community constructing its own library = higher costs than necessary
- Consolidation can take advantage of scale economies

**3. Inefficient Tax System:**
- Efficient tax requires higher tax rate on inelastic goods
- Goods inelastic at national level may be elastic at local level
- Capital: inelastic nationally, elastic locally
- Local governments impose little tax on capital → inefficient from national perspective

presentation_slides.title: More Disadvantages
presentation_slides.content:
**4. Loss of Scale Economies in Tax Collection:**
- Individual communities may not take advantage of scale economies
- Each community devotes resources to tax administration
- Savings possible through joint taxing authority

**5. Ineffectiveness of Redistributing Program (Equity Measures):**

**Scenario:**
- Tax and expenditure pattern favourable to the poor
- Transfers income to the poor
- Attracts more poor to this region
- Expels rich (taxpayers) out of this region

**Result:**
- Region left with small tax base
- Leads to abandonment of the program
- Redistribution efforts are undermined

presentation_slides.title: 7.3.1 Advantages of Decentralized System
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Tailoring Output to Local Tastes:**
- People in different regions have different tastes and preferences
- Centralized government provides same level of services throughout country
- Decentralized system: communities provide desired type and quantities
- Local government's greater proximity makes it more responsive

**2. Fostering Intergovernmental Competition:**
- Government managers lack incentives to minimize costs
- Private firms fail if they don't minimize costs
- Public managers can continue (no competition)
- But if citizens can change among communities:
  - Creates incentives for managers to produce efficiently
  - More responsive to citizens
  - Attract productive citizens

**3. Experimentation and Innovation:**
- For many policy questions, no one knows the right answer
- Best solution uncertain
- Each community can choose its own way
- Compare results

**Caveat:**
- Case in Ethiopia: One policy used across all regions
- Purely decentralized or centralized system cannot maximize social welfare
- There is some optimal level of federalism

presentation_slides.title: Unit 8: Economy, Environment and Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
Welcome to Unit 8! In this unit, we will explore:
- The link between economy and the environment
- Rural development and the environment
- Urban development and the environment
- Population, resources, and the environment
- Global warming and climate change
- Green economy and green growth
- Environment and climate change in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Section 8.1: Economy and the Environment
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Explain the link between economics, environment, rural development, urbanization, resources, and population

presentation_slides.title: Introduction to Economy and Environment
presentation_slides.content:
**Economics Definition:**
The study of the allocation of limited resources to satisfy human wants.

**Resources = Factors of Production:**
- Land
- Labour
- Capital
- Entrepreneurship
- Energy (sometimes specified separately)

**Key Economic Principle:**
- Economic resources are scarce (finite quantities)
- Claims on these resources are limitless
- Scarcity implies use is costly → Opportunity cost

**Environmental Resources:**
- Subset of economic resources
- Provide a broader set of goods and services
- Have become increasingly scarce as economic activity expands

presentation_slides.title: Classification of Environmental Resources
presentation_slides.content:
**Renewable Resources:**

**Biologically Renewable:**
- Forests
- Fish
- Animal population
- Biomass stock

**Physical Renewable:**
- Soil structure and fertility
- Ozone layer
- Earth's waste processing capacity

**Non-Renewable Resources:**
- Minerals
- Fossil fuels

**Key Point:**
- Both biological and physical renewable resources are potentially exhaustible
- Optimal and efficient growth must be pursued
- Sustainable development path needed

presentation_slides.title: Ecosystem and Human Behaviour
presentation_slides.content:
**Ecosystem:**
- Complex set of interdependencies between biological and physical systems
- Continually in a dynamic process of development and change

**Resilience of an Ecosystem:**
- Measure of extent to which it can be subjected to disturbances
- Without the system's parameters being changed

**Economic Behaviour:**
- Can reduce threshold levels of some system variables

**Implications:**
- Important for rates of depletion and harvesting of non-renewable resources

**Global Ecosystem Flow:**
- Raw materials and energy from planetary sources
→ Through the economy
→ To planetary sinks (receiving wastes)

**Underlying Pressure:**
- Growth of world population
- Industrial production

presentation_slides.title: 8.1.1 Rural Development and Environment
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Rural development is the process of improving the quality of life and economic wellbeing of people in rural areas.

**Includes:**
- Livelihoods
- Electricity provision
- Clean water
- Access roads
- Education

**Traditional Focus:**
- Exploitation of land-intensive natural resources
- Agriculture and forestry

**Major Issues Facing Agriculture:**
1. Use of pesticides
2. Loss of agricultural land fertility
3. Encroachment by rapid urbanization
4. Forest depletion
5. Declining soil fertility
6. Loss of topsoil
7. Desertification
8. Unsustainable water usage
9. Air pollution

presentation_slides.title: Population Pressure on Environment
presentation_slides.content:
**Effects of Population Pressure:**

**Intensification:**
- Soil erosion
- Natural depletion
- Destruction of soil structure (water holding capacity)
- Inorganic nutrients application unbalances soil structure

**Pollution from Inputs:**
- Fertilizer and pesticide pollution
- Increased resistance of pests
- Biodiversity loss
- Reduction of resilience
- Irreversible salination
- Water logging

**Extensification (Land Expansion):**
- Deforestation
- Desertification

**Poverty-Environment Nexus:**
- Low income households cut trees for firewood
- Cultivate marginal land
- Deforestation
- Overgrazing
- Soil exposed to flooding and erosion
- Cycle of rural poverty and environmental destruction

presentation_slides.title: 8.1.2 Urban Development and Environment
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Urban development is the social, cultural, economic and physical development of cities and the underlying causes of these processes.

**Covers:**
- Infrastructure for education, health, justice
- Solid waste, markets, street pavements
- Slums in large cities
- Informal settlements in towns and peri-urban areas

**Global Context:**
- World Bank estimates: >50% of population lives in urban areas globally
- By 2045: Urban population will increase to 6 billion

**Challenges:**
- Housing
- Power
- Water
- Transport
- Many governments ill-prepared to cope

presentation_slides.title: Environmental Costs of Urbanization
presentation_slides.content:
**Urban Pollution:**
- Tends to rise with national income levels first
- Then to fall

**High Environmental Costs:**
- Congestion
- Vehicular and industrial emissions
- Poorly ventilated household stoves

**Urban Poor:**
- Most affected by environmental degradation
- Inaccessibility of clean water
- Lack of sanitation
- Growing urban slums
- Malnutrition and poor health
- Reduced individual resistance to environmental hazards

**Solution:**
- Deploy clean technologies
- Produce less pollution and waste
- Use resources more efficiently

presentation_slides.title: 8.1.3 Population, Resources, and Environment
presentation_slides.content:
**World Population:**
- 2019: 7.7 billion
- 2025: 8.1 billion (projected)
- 2050: 9.6 billion (projected)
- Over 3/4 live in developing world

**Food Production Challenge:**
- Food production must increase by at least 50% in next 30 years
- Land is being unsustainably overexploited

**Rapid Population Growth Effects:**
1. Overuse of natural resources
2. Endangered welfare of future generations
3. Agricultural land holdings become smaller and unviable
4. No possibility of extensive cultivation (new land)
5. Many households continue to live in poverty

presentation_slides.title: Population-Environment Linkages
presentation_slides.content:
**Chain of Effects:**

Increasing Population Density → Disturbs land-man ratio → Inelastic supply of land → Disguised unemployment increases → Per capita productivity falls → Landless workers increase → Wages fall → Low per capita productivity reduces propensity to save and invest → Improved techniques not possible → Capital formation in agriculture suffers → Economy bogged down to subsistence level

**Other Problems:**
- Acute shortage of food products
- Increased imports → Balance of payment difficulties
- Over-cultivation of semi-arid areas → Desertification
- Migration to urban areas
- Severe air, water, and noise pollution

presentation_slides.title: Environmental Policy Requirements
presentation_slides.content:
**Concerns:**
- We may reach a limit to the number of people whose needs can be met by finite resources
- Continuing on present path of accelerating degradation will compromise ability of present and future generations

**What It Takes for Environmental Policies to Succeed:**

1. **Address issues of:**
   - Poverty
   - Landlessness
   - Lack of access to institutional resources

2. **Key Requirements:**
   - Insecure land tenure rights
   - Lack of credit and inputs
   - Absence of information

3. **Necessary Actions:**
   - Resource-augmenting investments
   - Preserve environmental assets for livelihoods
   - Firm commitment from government
   - Firm commitment from policy makers

presentation_slides.title: Section 8.2: Global Warming and Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Describe the link between global warming and climate change
- Define climate change
- Explain the causes, indicators, vulnerability, and impacts of climate change
- Examine the means to address climate change problems
- Appreciate policy measures Ethiopia is undertaking

presentation_slides.title: 8.2.1 Global Warming
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Global warming refers to increasing average air and ocean temperatures.

**Primary Greenhouse Gases:**
- Water vapour (H2O)
- Carbon dioxide (CO2)
- Nitrous oxide (N2O)
- Methane (CH4)
- Ozone (O3)

**Key Facts:**
- Trend began in mid-20th century
- Attributed largely to human activities:
  - Industrial activities
  - Forestry
  - Agriculture

**Emissions Increase:**
- Global GhG emissions increased by 70% between 1970 and 2004
- Three GhGs particularly increased:
  - CO2
  - CH4
  - N2O

**Figure 8.1:** Greenhouse gases and global warming

presentation_slides.title: Greenhouse Effect
presentation_slides.content:
**How It Works:**
1. GhGs trap long-wave radiation in the upper atmosphere
2. Raise atmospheric temperatures
3. Produce other changes in the climate system

**Pre-Industrial to 2011 Increases:**
- CO2: Increased by 40%
- CH4: Increased by 150%
- N2O: Increased by 20%

**Causes of Increase:**
- Burning of fossil fuels
- Reductions in carbon dioxide sinks (notably forests)

**Economic Activity-Energy-Emission Link:**
- Economic activity → Energy and material flows → GhG emissions
- Carbon emissions: Fossil fuel use
- Methane emissions: Agricultural activities, decomposition, waste disposal

presentation_slides.title: 8.2.2 Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition (IPCC):**
Climate change denotes a variation in the mean state of the climate persisting for an extended period (typically decades or longer) resulting from anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions.

**Key Point:**
Climate ≠ Weather

**Climate:**
- Average weather pattern over many years
- Expressed through: temperature, precipitation, wind

**Weather:**
- Short-term atmospheric conditions
- Events like temperature, rainfall, humidity
- Day to day or week to week

**Significance:**
- Climate change is one of the most urgent and complex challenges for societies and economies
- For developing countries like Ethiopia: Complicates existing challenges of poverty eradication

presentation_slides.title: 8.2.3 Causes of Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
**IPCC Predictions:**
- Probable rise in mean temperatures between 1.5°C and 4°C by 2099 (unless something is done)
- By 2016: Mean temperatures reached 1°C above pre-industrial level

**Causes:**
- Emissions of greenhouse gases triggering global warming

**Contribution to Greenhouse Effect:**
- CO2: 77% (largest)
- CH4: 14%
- N2O: 8%

**Sources:**
- **Developed Countries (USA):**
  - Burning fossil fuels for electricity, heat, transportation

- **Developing Countries:**
  - Deforestation contributes over 20% of harmful greenhouse gases
  - Also causes loss of valuable biodiversity
  - Loss of environmental services (cleaning air and water)

presentation_slides.title: 8.2.4 Indicators of Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
**According to IPCC:**
- Warming of the climate system is unequivocal

**Evidence:**
- Increases in global average air and ocean temperatures
- Widespread melting of snow and ice
- Rising global average sea level

**Specific Indicators:**
1. Unpredictable rain patterns
2. Too much and too little rain
3. Higher average air and ocean temperatures
4. Floods
5. Sea level rise
6. Melting of glaciers and ice caps
7. Cold days, cold nights, frosts becoming less frequent
8. Heat waves more common
9. Emergence of diseases (malaria in formerly cold climates)
10. Respiratory diseases more common

**Regional Changes:**
- Precipitation increased in: Australia, Central Asia, Mediterranean, Sahel, Western US
- Heavy rainfall and floods more common
- Storms and tropical cyclones more common
- Many regions: More frequent and more intense droughts

presentation_slides.title: 8.2.5 Impacts of Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
**Direct Impacts:**
- Physical and ecological environments
- Lagged effects → Additional indirect impacts

**Examples (Temperature rising over 2 degrees):**
- Heat waves
- Hurricanes and tornadoes
- Flooding from heightened rainfall
- Moisture stress from reduced rainfall
- Displacement from rising sea levels
- Losses of grasslands, farmlands, and marine ecosystems

**Long-Term Changes Affecting:**
- Agriculture
- Water
- Health
- Other sectors

**Semi-Arid and Arid Areas:**
- Area suitable for agriculture decreases
- Length of growing seasons decreases
- Yield potential decreases
- Food security affected, malnutrition exacerbated

**Coastal Areas:**
- Fisheries, mangroves, coral reefs degraded
- Threatened by sea level rise and storms

presentation_slides.title: Impacts on the Poor
presentation_slides.content:
**Who is Most Affected?**
- The very poor
- Depend mostly on natural resources (rain-fed agriculture)
- Housing is often poorly constructed
- Located in most environmentally stressed areas

**Health Dimension:**
- WHO estimated: 140,000 excess deaths per year (by 2004)
- Caused by: Diarrhoea, malaria, malnutrition
- Due to global warming since 1970s
- Mosquito-carried malaria migrating to higher altitudes
- Threatening Nairobi, Harare, and other cities

**Expected Impacts in Poorest Countries:**
1. Prolonged droughts
2. Expanded desertification
3. Increased severity of storms with heavy precipitation and flooding
4. Longer and more severe heat waves
5. Reduced summer river flow and water shortages
6. Decreased grain yields
7. Climate-induced spread of pests and diseases
8. Lost and contaminated groundwater
9. Deteriorated freshwater lakes
10. Coastal flooding
11. Loss of essential species (pollinators, soil organisms)
12. Forest fires

presentation_slides.title: 8.2.6 Vulnerability to Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Vulnerability is the degree to which a system is likely to experience harm as a result of exposure to climatic hazard.

**Depends On:**
1. Character, magnitude, and rate of climate variation
2. Sensitivity of the system
3. Adaptive capacity

**Dimensions:**
- Multi-dimensional
- Function of:
  - Biophysical outcomes (temperature, precipitation, topography, soil)
  - Socio-political factors
  - Level of economic development

**Who is Most Vulnerable?**
- Poor and marginalized people
- Live in low-income areas
- Houses made of mud, bamboo, straw
- Most vulnerable to extreme weather events
- Underrepresented at all levels of decision-making on climate issues

presentation_slides.title: Regional Vulnerability
presentation_slides.content:
**Most Vulnerable Regions:**
- Africa
- South Asia

**IPCC Four Highly Vulnerable Zones:**
1. **Sub-Saharan Africa:** Faces drying
2. **Asia:** Faces flooding
3. **Small Islands:** Face multiple sensitivities
4. **Arctic:** Face melting glaciers

**Specific Examples:**
- Small islands: Highly vulnerable to rising sea level
- Bangladesh: Highly prone to flooding
- Horn of Africa: Highly prone to droughts
- Dire Dawa (Ethiopia): Prone to flooding

**Poor Communities:**
- In high-risk areas
- More limited adaptive capacities
- More dependent on climate-sensitive resources
- Local water and food supplies

**International Obligation:**
- Poorest developing countries will be hit earliest and hardest
- Have contributed little to causing the problem
- Low incomes make it difficult to finance adaptation
- International community has obligation to support them

presentation_slides.title: 8.2.7 Means to Address Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
**Two Main Ways:**

**1. Mitigation:**
- Deals with the causes of climate change
- Reducing or stabilizing GhG concentrations
- Preventive policy approach
- Estimating costs and benefits of abatement
- Identifying socially optimal abatement targets
- Selecting policy instruments to minimize costs

**Mitigation Strategies:**
- Development of carbon markets
- Taxes on carbon
- Subsidies to encourage technological progress
- Long-term limits on greenhouse emissions

**Mitigation Mechanisms:**
- **REDD:** Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation
- **REDD-plus:** Enhanced incentives for re-establishing/maintaining forests with engagement of indigenous communities
- **CDM:** Clean Development Mechanism (from Kyoto Protocol 1997)

presentation_slides.title: Responsibility for Mitigation
presentation_slides.content:
**Developed Countries:**
- Historic responsibility
- Most greenhouse gases emitted historically
- Should take immediate steps to reduce emissions
- Develop new technologies for further reductions
- Support successful adaptation

**Developing Countries:**
- Share current and future responsibilities
- High fertility rates
- Rising average incomes
- Increasing greenhouse gas emissions

**Case Example - China:**
- Now the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter
- Lower on a per capita basis than most rich countries
- Must reduce emissions
- Without such action, reductions in developed world will only delay catastrophe

**Need for Assistance:**
- Poorer countries: More difficult to absorb costs of mitigation
- Low-income countries need technical and financial assistance
- International agreements:
  - Kyoto 1995
  - Paris 2015
  - Kigali 2016

**Synergy Required:**
- Labour-intensive production mechanisms
- Access to credit and extension service
- Provision of necessities and employment
- Soil and water conservation
- Defining property rights and land tenure
- Improvement in health and education

presentation_slides.title: Adaptation to Climate Change
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Adaptation is the process of enabling human and natural systems to adjust to the actual or expected climate stimuli or their effects.

**Related Term - Adaptive Capacity:**
- Ability of a system to adjust to climate change
- To moderate potential damage
- To take advantage of opportunities
- To cope with consequences

**Why Adaptation is Necessary:**
- Significant amount of climate change is already happening
- Essentially inevitable
- Lags in climate system mean climate change will unfold for many years
- Critical to protect livelihoods from climatic risks

**Forms of Adaptation:**
1. **Planned (Policy) Adaptation:** Undertaken by governments
2. **Autonomous (Private) Adaptation:** Undertaken by households, farms, firms

presentation_slides.title: Adaptation Strategies
presentation_slides.content:
**Four Classes of Adaptation Strategies:**

1. **Mobility:**
   - Avoids risks across space
   - People move away from danger areas

2. **Storage:**
   - Reduces risks experienced over time
   - Store food and resources for future

3. **Diversification:**
   - Reduces risks across assets owned by households or collectives
   - Diversify income sources
   - Diversify crops

4. **Communal Pool:**
   - Joint ownership of assets and resources
   - Sharing of wealth, labour, or incomes
   - Mobilization and use of resources held collectively during scarcity

**Key Point:**
Adaptation is a universal condition of humanity
- Human adaptability is as old as human societies
- Vital characteristic ensuring survival of cultures

**Challenge:**
- Climate change presents newer, unique, and complex challenges

presentation_slides.title: Section 8.3: Green Economy and Green Growth
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Define green economy
- Explain green growth
- Identify the sources of renewable energy

presentation_slides.title: Green Economy
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
A green economy is an economy that results in:
- Improved human wellbeing and social equity
- Significantly reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcities

**Characteristics:**
1. Low carbon
2. Resource efficient
3. Socially inclusive

**How It Works:**
- Economic growth driven by public and private investments that:
  - Reduce carbon emissions and pollution
  - Enhance energy and resource efficiency
  - Prevent loss of biodiversity and ecosystem services

**Expected Outcomes:**
- Investment and innovation underpin sustained growth
- Give rise to new economic opportunities

**Relevance:**
- Not only relevant to advanced economies
- Also a key catalyst for growth and poverty eradication in developing countries

presentation_slides.title: Green Growth
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition (OECD):**
Green growth is "fostering economic growth and development, while ensuring that natural assets continue to provide the resources and environmental services on which our wellbeing relies."

**Rationale:**
- Growing risks to development as growth continues to erode natural capital

**Consequences of Eroding Natural Capital:**
- Increased water scarcity
- Worsening resource bottlenecks
- Greater pollution
- Climate change
- Unrecoverable biodiversity loss

**Sources of Renewable Energy:**
1. Solar
2. Biomass and biofuel
3. Geothermal
4. Hydroelectricity
5. Tidal
6. Wind-driven

**Motive for Renewable Energy:**
- Perceived scarcity of fossil fuels
- Potential for peak oil (rising demand, declining production)
- Climate change concerns

sections.section_title: Overview of Environment and Climate Change in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Section 8.4: Overview in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Gain insight into national policies to address climate change in Ethiopia

presentation_slides.title: Environment and Climate Change in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**Geography:**
- East African country
- Immense geographical diversity
- Topographical variation

**Vulnerability:**
- One of the most vulnerable countries to future climate change
- Last 100 years: Recurrent drought, famine, food aid

**Major Environmental Issues:**
- Soil erosion
- Land degradation
- Increased crop cultivation in marginal areas
- Livestock grazing pressure

**Consequences:**
- Agricultural landscapes undergone unprecedented changes
- Unsustainable direction:
  - Land degradation
  - Biodiversity loss
  - Low agricultural productivity

presentation_slides.title: Policy Responses in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
**2007: National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA)**

**2011: Nationally Appropriate Mitigation Actions (NAMA)**

**Key Findings from NAPA/NAMA:**
- Key underlying causes of vulnerability:
  1. Dependence on rain-fed agriculture
  2. Poor water resource development
  3. High population growth rate

**Sectors Most Vulnerable:**
1. Agriculture
2. Health
3. Transport
4. Natural resources
5. Energy
6. Industry

presentation_slides.title: Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) Strategy
presentation_slides.content:
**Initiative Started:** 2011

**Vision:**
- Carbon-neutral growth
- Energy-efficient development trajectory

**Objectives:**
1. Climate change adaptation (climate resilience)
2. Mitigation (green economy)

**Goal:**
- Achieve middle-income status by 2025
- Initially raises GDP per capita to $1000 USD

**Green Legacy Initiative (June 2020):**
- Tree-planting campaign
- Aimed at curbing effects of climate change and deforestation

**Goals of Green Legacy:**
- Preventing flooding
- Preventing food insecurity
- Preventing environment-related conflicts
- Addressing other adverse effects of climate change
- Addressing deforestation

**Achievement:**
- 4.1 billion trees planted by August 2020

**Responsible Agency:**
- Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
